question.leadin: This poet's rivalry with John Keats was so intense that he used the poem Don Juan [don JOO-an] to mock him after death, claiming that Keats had died from reading a bad review of his work instead of from tuberculosis.
question.text: Name this English Romantic poet. Keats was convinced that this nobleman had bought good reviews for works like Childe Harold's Pilgrimage.
question.answerHtml: Lord Byron (accept George Gordon, Lord Byron; accept George Gordon Noel Byron, sixth Baron Byron)
question.clue: This commander who, in April 1824, died of a fever in Missolonghi before he could execute an attack on Lepanto.

swap.leadin: The murders of the "canonical five" victims are believed to be linked and the work of this man.
swap.text: Name this unknown serial killer, who committed murders in the White Chapel district of London during the late 1800s.
swap.clue: This serial killer thought to have killed at least five women in the 1880s. The Whitechapel Vigilance Committee was formed to try to catch this killer.

question.leadin: Name some 20th century British Prime Ministers.
question.text: Churchill's predecessor was this man, who is most well-known for claiming Europe would be at peace after signing the Munich Agreement.
question.clue: Edvard Benes was notably not present at the conference that this man and Edouard Daladier are most well-known for attending.

swap.text: This English king opposed Cromwell during the Civil War. He was later executed.
swap.clue: This ruler was depicted "at the hunt" by his court painter, Anthony van Dyck.

question.text: The other leader featured in The Plumb-Pudding in Danger is William Pitt the Younger, who held this position. Another man in this position, Clement Atlee, is depicted in the cartoon No Place for a Pole Squatter.
question.answerHtml: British Prime Minister [accept Prime Minister of the United Kingdom or equivalents]

swap.leadin: Prince Rupert of the Rhine was a cavalry commander for one side during this conflict, during which the battles of Marston Moor and Naseby were fought.
swap.text: Name this conflict, where the Roundheads fought the Cavaliers. Charles I was executed after this conflict.
swap.clue: This conflict's second phase saw the defeat of Scottish forces at Preston, after which the victorious commander perpetrated the massacre at Drogheda to punish Irish supporters of his enemies.

question.leadin: This man served as the last Prime Minister of the Liberal Party before it was superseded by the Labour Party.
question.text: Name this man who led Britain through the last half of World War I and who represented Britain at the Paris Peace conference.
question.clue: This man served as the Minister of Munitions and had a seven year stint as the Chancellor of the Exchequer.

swap.text: This battle which saw Harold Godwinson emerge victorious is considered the end of the Viking Age. A legend states that at this battle a Viking warrior held off the entire Anglo-Saxon army.
swap.clue: According to legend, a single soldier held up one side's advance across a bridge over the Derwent River until an English soldier speared him from under the bridge.

question.text: The victor at the Battle of Eddington was this king who employed the chronicler Asser and issued a law code called the Doom Book.
question.clue: Although he is not William the Conqueror, this man created a doom book, and this man fought against Ivar the Boneless at the Battle of Ashdown.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about the search for El Dorado.
swap.text: Though he definitely didn't reach El Dorado, this Englishman still wildly exaggerated his finds in his The Discovery of Guiana. He founded a colony whose residents included Virginia Dare.
swap.answerHtml: Sir Walter Raleigh (The colony is the Roanoake colony.)
swap.clue: Accounts of an ill-fated conquistador likely based on Juan Martin de Albujar inspired this man to lead an expedition in South America to find El Dorado.

question.leadin: During this man's term, George Soros worked over his country's financial system and forced him to withdraw from the Exchange Rate Mechanism on "Black Wednesday."
question.text: Name this Conservative British PM of the 1990s who fashioned the "Back to Basics" campaign. He won the so-called "Soap Box election" after he went to the streets and literally stood on soapboxes to deliver his message.
question.clue: This politician signed the Downing Street Declaration with Albert Reynolds.

swap.leadin: This movement was named for a bill written by Samuel Lovett in 1838.
swap.text: What British working-class group called for reforms like annual parliamentary elections and universal suffrage for men?
swap.clue: A march on the Westgate Hotel led by John Frost to free supporters of this movement culminated in the Newport Rising.

question.leadin: This legislation restricted the right of church officials to excommunicate criminals, requiring the consent of a royal official, and held that vacant church offices in the king's domain devolved to the king.
question.text: Name this list of sixteen articles aiming to combat so-called "criminous clerks" and weaken the power of the church, promulgated in England.
question.clue: Condemned at Sens in Burgundy by Pope Alexander III, they were approved at the council of Westminster by the bishops.

swap.text: In another media reporting mishap, the BBC World Service prematurely announced victory at this first land battle during the war, which took place on Choiseul Sound on East Falkland.
swap.clue: This major battle of the Falklands War saw 3 Commando Brigade attack with the support of the HMS Arrow and defeat the defending Argentine forces.

question.leadin: In Nennius's History of the Britons, a fight between two of these creatures serves as a metaphor for Celtic resistance to the Saxon invasion.
question.text: Name this creature depicted on Henry Tudor's banners at the Battle of Bosworth Field as a reference to the 7th-century king of Gwynedd Cadwaladr ap Cadwallon ("GWIN-eth cad-WA-la-der ap cad-WA-lon").
question.answerHtml: Welsh dragon [or ddraig Cymraeg (“thraig cum-raig”); or ddraig goch (“goh”); accept red dragon; accept white dragon; accept ddraig gwyn]

swap.leadin: This movement's name refers to a series of institutions mentioned in the Book of Daniel, one of which ended with the beheading of Charles I of England.
swap.text: Name this movement which advocated for reforms and the abolishing of tithes in the Barebones Parliament. A leader of this movement, Thomas Harrison, was later hung, drawn and quartered.

question.leadin: Answer the following about incorrect predictions based on the Book of Revelation in early modern Britain.
question.text: In the 1590s, this Scottish scholar calculated from Revelation that the Apocalypse would happen either in 1688 or in 1700. This scholar introduced a multiplication technique called his namesake "bones."
question.answerHtml: John Napier of Merchiston [or Ioannes Neper; accept Napier’s rods or Napier’s bones]

swap.leadin: This system of church governance provided its name to the "Peace Party" in the Long Parliament, who opposed the radical "Independents."
swap.text: Name this system of church government that was implemented in Scotland by Andrew Melville after being devised by John Knox.

question.leadin: This 1517 event turned violent after Dr. Bell made a speech that incited this event, inviting "Englishmen to cherish and defend themselves, and to hurt and grieve aliens for the common weal."
question.text: Name this riot, dubbed an "Evil" version of the namesake holiday, in which xenophobic riots led to looting of foreigners' houses.

swap.leadin: His major work was compiled by Richard Hosley.
swap.text: Name this medieval writer and historian whose namesake chronicles were used by William Shakespeare to write Cymbeline, Macbeth and other plays.
